title: A thank-you before the first bite

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when did you last think about everyone who made your dinner possible?
options: then you’re already halfway into this story. listen.
most of us don’t. this rabbi did. listen.
me too, most days. listen, this one is kind.

steps.line: The Talmud tells of a rabbi, Ben Zoma. One day he stood high on the steps of the Temple Mount and looked down at a huge, busy crowd.
He said a blessing out loud: “Blessed is the One who created all these people to serve me.”

steps.q: “All these people, to serve me”? Ben Zoma explains with Adam, the first human. What did Adam have to do before he could eat bread?
o: Every step himself, from plow to oven
Wait for God to send bread each day
Gather wild fruit; bread didn’t exist yet
steps.why: The Talmud lists eleven steps: plow, sow, reap, bind, thresh, winnow, sort, grind, sift, knead, bake (Berakhot 58a). Ben Zoma woke to find all of it done for him.

steps.line: He explained. The first human had to do it all alone: plow, sow, reap, thresh, grind, sift, knead and bake. Only then could he eat.
“And I get up in the morning,” said Ben Zoma, “and find it all ready for me.” The farmer, the miller, the baker, the weaver. All of them.

steps.q: Ben Zoma is famous for another question: “Who is rich?” What’s his answer?
o: One who gives the most away
One who is happy with their portion
One who owes nothing to anyone
steps.why: Mishnah Avot 4:1. It’s the same eye as the bread blessing: notice what’s already in front of you.

steps.line: He also said: a good guest says, “How much trouble my host took for me!” A bad guest says, “What trouble? I only ate one piece of bread.”

steps.q: The bad guest isn’t lying: he really only ate one piece of bread. So what’s wrong with what he says?
o: He should have eaten more, to be polite
He forgot to thank the host by name
He counts what he took, not what it cost
steps.why: The good guest sees the work behind the meal; the bad one sees only his own plate. Same bread, different eyes.

steps.q: Before an apple, the blessing ends “who creates the fruit of the tree.” Before a glass of water, how does it end?
o: “By whose word all things came to be”
steps.why: That’s shehakol, said over water and anything without its own blessing (Mishnah Berakhot, chapter 6). The ending fits the food; the opening never changes.

steps.line: Today, before an apple or a glass of water, many Jews pause to say a short blessing, a bracha. It isn’t said to the food. It’s said to the source.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. a bracha opens the same way every time: baruch atah adonai, blessed are you. then the ending changes with the food: who brings forth bread from the earth, who creates the fruit of the tree.

the rabbis noticed one psalm says the earth is god’s, and another says the earth was given to people. their answer: both. the blessing is the hinge. before it, the apple is still god’s. after it, it’s been given to you.

steps.q: Ben Zoma blessed God for “all these people.” Why thank God for work that people did?
o: He saw God at work through all those hands
The farmers and bakers were Temple servants
Thanking people directly wasn’t done then
steps.why: Many readers hear it this way: the blessing goes to the One who made a world where a crowd of hands feeds you, and the noticing goes to them.

today.say: today, before your first bite of something, pause for two seconds. you could say a short blessing, in hebrew or your own words, or just think of one hand that brought it to you. watch, learn or join in, it’s your choice.
options: two seconds. that’s a good guest.
perfect. there’s a blessing for that too: by whose word all things came to be.

card.keepWhy: Notice the hands before you bite.
sources: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 58a (Ben Zoma sees a crowd on a step of the Temple Mount; ‘Blessed… who created all these to serve me’; the labors of the first human for bread: plowed, sowed, reaped, bound, threshed, winnowed, selected, ground, sifted, kneaded, baked; and for a garment; ‘and I rise and find all this ready for me’; the good guest and the bad guest; the lesson paraphrases: the bread list is shortened from eleven labors to eight, the clothing list is folded into ‘the weaver’, and the two guests’ words are shortened)

Psalms 24:1 (“The earth is the LORD’S, and the fulness thereof,” JPS 1917); Psalms 115:16 (“the earth hath He given to the children of men,” JPS 1917); Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35a (the two verses reconciled: before and after the blessing)
Mishnah Berakhot 6:1 (the blessings for fruit of the tree and for bread); 6:3 and 6:8 (shehakol, ‘by whose word all things came to be’, also said over water)
